subject: Advanced Science
central_question: How can differences in movement through phases and differences in boiling points be used to separate and purify the components of mixtures?
in_scope_units: 8.1 Chromatography: history, meaning, principle, and applications

8.2.1 Fractional Distillation: principle, apparatus, fractionating column, and procedure
8.2.2 Difference between fractional distillation and simple distillation
8.2.3 Fractional distillation of crude oil and collection of useful fractions
Questions 1-15 on chromatography and fractional distillation

known_pitfalls.claim: Chromatography separates substances because they have different boiling points.
known_pitfalls.correction: Chromatography separates components because they move at different rates through a stationary phase under the influence of a mobile phase, often because their adsorption or partition tendencies differ.

known_pitfalls.claim: The solvent packed inside a chromatography column is the stationary phase.
known_pitfalls.correction: Silica gel or alumina packed in the column is the stationary phase; the flowing solvent or eluent is the mobile phase.

known_pitfalls.claim: The component that comes out of a column first is the one most strongly adsorbed on the stationary phase.
known_pitfalls.correction: A component that comes out first interacts less strongly with the stationary phase and is carried more readily by the mobile phase.

known_pitfalls.claim: A fractionating column works only by cooling the vapour once.
known_pitfalls.correction: Its large surface area permits repeated condensation and vaporization, progressively enriching the rising vapour in the lower-boiling component.

known_pitfalls.claim: Simple distillation is preferred when two miscible liquids have very close boiling points.
known_pitfalls.correction: The chapter uses fractional distillation when boiling points differ by less than 25°C; simple distillation is suitable when the difference is at least about 25°C.

known_pitfalls.claim: Every fraction in a crude-oil column condenses at the same height.
known_pitfalls.correction: The column is hotter near the bottom and cooler near the top, so fractions condense at different heights according to their boiling ranges.

recommended_example_progression: Use Questions 1-3 to establish the meaning of chromatography and distinguish stationary and mobile phases.
Use Questions 4-6 and Fig. 8.1 to identify silica gel or alumina, the eluent, and the reason components move at different rates.
Use Question 10 to infer that a compound emerging first interacts less strongly with the stationary phase.
Use Questions 7-9 with Fig. 8.2 to explain fractional distillation and the role of the fractionating column.
Use Question 11 with ethanol at 78°C and water at 100°C to select fractional distillation.
Use Questions 12-14 to explain repeated condensation and vaporization and to contrast simple with fractional distillation.
Use the crude-oil application in Section 8.2.3 to connect boiling ranges with fractions collected at different heights.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The supplied chapter ends with a section titled 'Questions', containing conceptual, application, and assertion-reason items on chromatography and fractional distillation.

beyond_the_textbook: Chromatography can be coupled with detectors that help identify very small amounts of separated substances in environmental, food, and medical samples.
In thin-layer chromatography, a thin adsorbent coating replaces the packed column, but separation still depends on different interactions with stationary and mobile phases.
Industrial distillation columns use trays or packing to create repeated contact between rising vapour and descending liquid, following the same principle as the laboratory fractionating column.
Crude-oil fractions are mixtures grouped by boiling range rather than single pure compounds.
Vacuum distillation lowers boiling temperatures and is useful for high-boiling substances that might decompose at their normal boiling points.
